content: 1. The 2006 WHO guidelines on the treatment of HIV in infants and children emphasize the importance of universal access to antiretroviral therapy (ART) and provide recommendations for a public health approach. 2. Gilks et al. (2006) discuss the WHO public health approach to ART in resource-limited settings, highlighting strategies to improve access and outcomes. 3. The 2013 WHO consolidated guidelines on the use of antiretroviral drugs for treating and preventing HIV infection provide updated recommendations for a public health approach. 4. The 90-90-90 initiative sets ambitious global targets to end the AIDS epidemic by ensuring 90% of people living with HIV know their status, 90% of those diagnosed receive ART, and 90% of those on ART achieve viral suppression. 5. The WHO Global Health Sector Strategy for HIV (2016–2021) outlines a comprehensive plan to accelerate progress toward ending the HIV epidemic. 6. The WHO Handbook for Guideline Development (2nd edition, 2014) provides a framework for creating evidence-based health guidelines. 7. A WHO consultation report on HIV treatment among adolescents addresses the unique challenges and strategies for managing HIV in this population. 8. The PRISMA statement offers a standardized approach for transparent reporting of systematic reviews and meta-analyses. 9. The GRADE guidelines provide a systematic method for rating the quality of evidence and strength of recommendations in clinical practice. 10. Studies such as the SMART trial and others have evaluated the clinical outcomes of ART initiation in treatment-naïve individuals and those not receiving ART at baseline. 11. Research by Cohen et al. (2011) demonstrated that early ART significantly reduces the risk of HIV transmission in serodiscordant couples. 12. Studies have consistently shown that baseline viral load, CD4 count, and early virologic response are critical predictors of long-term treatment success and virologic failure. 13. Collaborative analyses of HIV cohort studies have provided evidence on the optimal timing of ART initiation to improve clinical outcomes and reduce mortality. 14. The CASCADE collaboration and other studies have explored the impact of early versus delayed ART initiation on immune recovery and clinical progression. 15. Research has highlighted the feasibility of achieving high CD4 counts after prolonged ART, particularly in patients starting treatment with higher baseline CD4 levels. 16. The HIV-CAUSAL collaboration has examined the effects of combined ART on overall mortality and AIDS-related illnesses. 17. Studies in resource-limited settings, such as those in rural South Africa and China, have shown that high ART coverage is associated with reduced HIV transmission and improved public health outcomes. 18. Mathematical models have demonstrated the cost-effectiveness and health benefits of earlier ART eligibility and expanded treatment coverage. 19. UNAIDS reports have documented the transformative impact of the global AIDS response on public health and development goals. 20. Late presentation to care remains a persistent challenge, with significant economic and clinical implications for patients and health systems. 21. The PARTNER study and other trials have provided robust evidence that individuals on suppressive ART have a negligible risk of transmitting HIV through condomless sex. 22. The TEMPRANO trial in Africa demonstrated the benefits of early ART initiation and isoniazid preventive therapy in reducing morbidity and mortality. 23. Observational cohort studies in China and other regions have confirmed the effectiveness of ART in preventing HIV transmission in serodiscordant couples. 24. Research has also focused on the association between ART timing and the normalization of immune status, as well as the impact of payer type on HIV disease stage at ART initiation in the U.S. 25. The INSIGHT START study group has provided compelling evidence supporting the initiation of ART in asymptomatic individuals with higher CD4 counts to improve survival and reduce disease progression.
